To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the fourth generation leptons and quark are not excluded by the current Z-boson precision measurements, provided that (i) the mass of the neutrino is about 50 GeV, (ii) the mixing with the neutrino of the first three generation is negligibly small and (iii) the Higgs boson is invisible, due to its predominant decay into the pair of the 50 GeV fourth generation neutrino.

if the mass of the neutrino of the fourth generation is about 50 GeV, then the Higgs to invisible decay rate is about 2% and that the Higgs to bbbar decay rate is about one order of magnitude smaller than the Higgs-to-4th-generation-neutrinos decay rate.

the fourth generation leptons and quark, if they exist, must have a mass of about 200 GeV, while the fourth neutrino must have a mass in the range from 50 to 70 GeV, and the mass difference between the fourth neutrino and the fourth charged lepton must be in the range from about 10 to 20 GeV, and that the mixing of the fourth neutrinos with the neutrinos in the first three generations should be negligibly small.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions. What is the probability of the fourth generation of fermions? Is it consistent with the data? What is the probability that the mass of a new lightest neutrino is around fifty GeV? What are the consequences of the fourth generation for the Standard Model? What are the implications for the LHC and the ILC?

the following questions: 1) Can one detect the fourth generation of fermions at LHC, if its neutrino is light and has negligible mixing with the neutrino of the first three generation? 2) How to detect the invisible Higgs bosons, if they exist?

the following topics: (i) The possibility of the fourth generation of quarks and leptons, (ii) the search for the Higgs boson in the Standard Model with the fourth generation, (iii) the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model with four generations, (iv) the study of CP-violation in four-generation leptons, and (v) the study of four-generation quarks in the context of the CP violation in K and B decays.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fourth generation is not excluded by precision Z-bosons data, provided that the Higgs boson is invisible.

the Standard Model Higgless scenario, in which the Higgs mass is around 100 GeV and the fourth generation of quarks and leptons is not excluded, would require a new mechanism to explain the observed top quark mass, as well as a new mechanism to generate a large enough mass for the fourth neutrino.
, if the fourth generation of quarks and leptons exists and the fourth neutrino mass is around 50~GeV, the discovery of the Higgs boson would require a dedicated search for the invisible decays.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fourth generation neutrino with the mass around 50 Gev is a good candidate to be a dominant decay mode for the Higgs, and that the Higgs to 50 GeV-neutrino searches are complementary to the direct search for the Higgs at LEP2 and the Tevatron.
if the fourth generation is not excluded by precision Z measurements, then it is very difficult to discover the Standard Model Higg boson at the LHC, unless the Higgs is light (less than 150 GeV).
if a 50 GeV heavy neutrino is found in the future, then the Standard Model Higg boson would have to be invisible.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the invisible decay mode of the Standard Model-like Higgs boson can be a powerful tool in the search for the fourth generation of fermions.
the invisible Higgs bosons are not a new phenomenon.
the Higgs boson would be very hard to detect at the LHC, even if it has a mass of 100 GeV, in the scenario of a light 50 GeV fourth generation neutrino, and a light fourth generation down-type quark.
